title: Classic Northern Italian Grapes in Depth
quiz.0.question: Why does Nebbiolo excel almost only in Piemonte?
quiz.0.options.0: Extremely demanding of terroir (elevation, exposure, soil, climate)
quiz.0.explanation: Nebbiolo is extremely demanding of terroir: it needs the right elevation, sunny exposures (south to south-west), calcareous marl soils (Tortonian/Serravallian) and a long growing season, so it performs perfectly only in certain parts of Piemonte.
quiz.1.question: What is Barbera's defining trait?
quiz.1.explanation: Barbera has high acidity and low tannin, which makes it a perfect partner for Italian food.
quiz.2.question: Which DOCG mainly uses Sangiovese Grosso?
quiz.2.explanation: Montalcino's Sangiovese (locally called Brunello, traditionally classed as Grosso) is the only grape permitted in Brunello di Montalcino DOCG; the wines are concentrated and tannic and must be aged 5 years (Riserva 6).
quiz.3.question: Why is Aglianico called the "Nebbiolo of the South"?
quiz.3.options.1: Very high tannin and acidity, needs long ageing
quiz.3.explanation: Aglianico resembles Nebbiolo in its very high tannin and acidity and its need for long ageing; both are the noblest grapes of their regions, complex and with remarkable ageing potential.

slides.2.title: 👑 Nebbiolo — Grape Profile and Terroir Needs
slides.2.content:
The "king of the fog" (nebbia = fog), Italy's noblest red grape — concentrated mainly in Piemonte, and also found in Lombardy's Valtellina (Chiavennasca) and Valle d'Aosta (Picotendro), it is extremely demanding of terroir; a paradox: pale in colour yet with a formidable structure, it needs 5-30 years to show its true face

🏔️

Demanding Terroir

Elevation: 200-450 m (too low is too hot, too high is too cold)

Exposure: south to south-west (Barolo) / south to south-east (Barbaresco)

Soils: Tortonian calcareous marl (more perfumed and elegant) / Serravallian sandstone and compacted marl (more structured)

Climate: spring fogs keep humidity, autumn fogs delay harvest and lengthen ripening

Ripening: very late (mid to late October), vulnerable to bad weather

🍷

Structure & How the Flavour Evolves

Colour: pale garnet with an orange rim (light in appearance, powerful in substance)

Tannin: very high, tight and astringent when young

Acidity: high

Young (<5 years): red fruit, rose, tannins tight and unbalanced

Mature (5-15 years): dried flowers, leather, truffle, a complete structure

Aged (15+ years): tar, spice, chocolate, peak complexity

slides.3.title: ⚔️ Barolo vs Barbaresco — King and Queen
slides.3.content:
One grape, two souls — soil differences shape the power of Barolo, the "king of wines", and the elegance of Barbaresco, the "queen of wines"

👑 Barolo DOCG — King of Wines

Soils: in the west, La Morra and Barolo village are mainly Tortonian calcareous marl (more perfumed); in the east, Serralunga and Monforte are mainly Serravallian sandstone and compacted marl (more structured)

Elevation: about 250-450 m

Style: powerful, with massive tannins and a complex structure, needs long ageing

Ageing: 38 months (18 in wood); Riserva 62 months

Villages: 11 (Barolo, La Morra, Serralunga...)

Famous MGAs: Cannubi, Brunate, Bussia, Vigna Rionda

Schools: traditionalists (large old Slavonian casks) vs modernists (French barriques)

👸 Barbaresco DOCG — Queen of Wines

Soils: mainly Tortonian calcareous marl (elegant and refined)

Elevation: about 200-350 m, closer to the Tanaro, warmer and earlier ripening

Style: elegant, silky, finely floral, approachable earlier than Barolo

Ageing: 26 months (9 in wood); Riserva 50 months

Villages: 3 (Barbaresco, Neive, Treiso)

Famous MGAs: Asili, Rabajà, Sorì Tildìn, Martinenga

Leading producers: Gaja, Bruno Giacosa, Marchesi di Grésy

slides.4.title: 🍒 Barbera — Grape Profile and Style Revolution
slides.4.content:
One of Italy's most widely planted red grapes, Piemonte's everyday hero — high acidity + low tannin make it a natural partner for Italian food; in 1982 Giacomo Bologna launched the modern quality Barbera revolution

📊 Grape Profile

Acidity: high, keeping bright acidity even in warm areas

Tannin: low to medium (thin skins, smooth rather than astringent)

Colour: deep purple-red (rich in anthocyanins, holds its colour)

Alcohol: 12.5-15% (depending on area and vintage)

Flavours: red/black cherry, plum, spice, black pepper

Character: high acid + low tannin = Italy's most food-versatile red

🍷 How the Style Evolved

Traditional style (before 1980):
An unoaked everyday wine, light and easy, its acidity cutting through rich Piemontese food — a staple of the farmhouse table

The 1982 revolution:
Giacomo Bologna's "Bricco dell'Uccellone": low yields + French barriques proved Barbera could make top wines

Modern style:
Full-bodied and complex, ageing 5-10 years; Nizza DOCG (2014) crowns Barbera

slides.5.title: 🏆 Barbera Appellation Hierarchy
slides.5.content:
Barbera's quality pyramid in Piemonte — Nizza DOCG, independent since 2014, is the peak of Barbera, its strict rules giving "little Barolo" quality

💎 Nizza DOCG — The Peak (independent since 2014)
Split from Barbera d'Asti with the strictest rules: 100% Barbera, 18 months of ageing (6 in wood), Riserva 30 months (12 in wood), minimum 13% alcohol, limited to 18 municipalities around Nizza Monferrato; the most concentrated, complex and age-worthy
⭐ Barbera d'Asti Superiore DOCG — High Quality
Barbera d'Asti became a DOCG in 2008; Superiore requires 14 months of ageing (6 in oak), balanced and elegant
🍷 Barbera d'Alba DOC — The Powerful Version
Around Alba, sharing top sites with Barolo/Barbaresco; Superiore aged 12 months (4 in oak), fuller-bodied
🌿 Barbera del Monferrato DOC — Everyday and Approachable
The Monferrato hills in the provinces of Asti and Alessandria; light and fruity for everyday drinking, can be made frizzante, the entry level of Barbera; the Superiore level is a DOCG
slides.6.title: 🍬 Dolcetto — The Underrated "Little Sweet One"
slides.6.content:
Its name means "little sweet one", yet the wine is fully dry — an early-ripening grape that kept Piemonte estates' cash flowing while Nebbiolo aged, and a daily companion on local tables

📊 Grape Profile

Ripening: early (picked mid-September, about a month before Nebbiolo)

Acidity: low to medium, clearly lower than Barbera

Tannin: medium to high (but soft in texture, unlike Nebbiolo's grip)

Flavours: black cherry, plum, liquorice; a signature slightly bitter almond finish

Alcohol: 11.5-13%

Hallmark: the bitter-almond finish is Dolcetto's clearest varietal marker

🎭 Its Role in Piemonte

Status: planted on lesser sites, with the best reserved for Nebbiolo, yet indispensable

Dogliani DOCG: widely seen as the best Dolcetto area; Superiore is more powerful and complex

Dolcetto d'Alba DOC: the most common, light and fruity, best young within 1-3 years, an everyday food wine

Ovada DOCG: fuller-bodied with more tannin, a speciality of the province of Alessandria

slides.7.title: 🍇 Corvina — The Four Steps of Appassimento
slides.7.content:
The soul of Valpolicella and the heart of appassimento — the same Corvina grapes, made in different ways, create a complete four-step ladder from light everyday wine to legendary richness, Italy's most distinctive use of a single grape

🌿 Valpolicella DOC — Fresh and Light
A blend of Corvina (45-95%) + Rondinella (5-30%) made from fresh grapes: light, fruity, with marked acidity, drunk young as an everyday food wine
🍷 Valpolicella Ripasso DOC — Re-passed over the Pomace
Refermented on Amarone / Recioto pomace (ripasso = "re-passed"), giving more body (Superiore minimum 13%) and much more complexity, often called "baby Amarone"
💎 Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG — The Dry Dried-Grape Legend
Grapes dried for several months to concentrate the sugar, fermented to dryness, minimum 14% alcohol (often 15-16% or more), aged at least 2 years (Riserva 4); dried fruit, chocolate, leather
🍯 Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG — The Sweet Dried-Grape Wine
The sweet forerunner of Amarone, with fermentation stopped to keep residual sugar; black fruit, chocolate and honey, richly sweet yet elegant, one of Verona's oldest wines, with strong ageing potential

🍇 Corvina's Traits

Thick skins (resisting rot, suitable for months of drying), high acidity, medium tannin — three traits that make Corvina the perfect vehicle for appassimento. Its blending partner Rondinella adds colour and aroma; Molinara has not been a required variety since 2003 and is now used far less.
slides.8.title: 🌟 Sangiovese — Grape Profile and Clonal Diversity
slides.8.content:
"Blood of Jupiter" (Sanguis Jovis), Italy's most widely planted red grape (71,000 ha) — with huge clonal and terroir variation, from everyday Chianti to long-lived Brunello, one grape covers the full quality spectrum of Italian red wine

📊

Grape Profile

Area planted: 71,000 ha, Italy's most planted variety

Acidity: high

Tannin: high (but varying greatly with clone and terroir)

Colour: medium to pale garnet with an orange rim

Alcohol: 12-14.5%

Flavours: sour cherry, tomato, tea leaf; with age: leather, tobacco, spice

🧬

Clones and Local Names

Sangiovese Grosso:
Traditionally the larger-berried group was called Grosso; in Montalcino Sangiovese is called Brunello, and Brunello di Montalcino DOCG must be 100% Sangiovese — concentrated, tannic and long-lived

Sangiovese Piccolo:
Traditionally the smaller-berried group was called Piccolo, but today the focus is on selecting individual clones and this split is no longer precise

Prugnolo Gentile:
Montepulciano's local name for Sangiovese, the lead grape of Vino Nobile DOCG, balanced and elegant

slides.9.title: 🏆 Sangiovese Quality Pyramid
slides.9.content:
Sangiovese's quality pyramid — from entry-level Chianti to the peak of Brunello, one grape across different soils and winemaking shows the fullest range of Italian red wine

🏆 Brunello di Montalcino DOCG — The Peak
100% Sangiovese (locally called Brunello), aged at least 5 years after harvest (2 in oak); Riserva 6 years; varied soils (galestro, alberese, clay); the Biondi-Santi family built its reputation in the late 19th century
⭐ Chianti Classico DOCG Gran Selezione — Top Level
The top tier since 2014, using only grapes from the estate's own vineyards, aged at least 30 months, with the Gallo Nero (black rooster) seal, highly complex
🍷 Chianti Classico DOCG Riserva / Vino Nobile DOCG
Chianti Classico Riserva (24 months of ageing), Vino Nobile (70%+ Prugnolo Gentile, 2 years of ageing), Rosso di Montalcino DOC (the earlier-drinking version of Brunello)
🌿 Chianti DOCG / Morellino di Scansano — Everyday Range
Chianti DOCG (70%+ Sangiovese, light and easy, many sub-areas); Morellino di Scansano DOCG (Maremma coast, fruity), everyday partners for pasta
slides.10.title: 🌋 Aglianico — The Nebbiolo of the South
slides.10.content:
"The Nebbiolo of the South" — very high tannin + very high acidity + volcanic minerality, southern Italy's noblest red grape, very late-ripening, with volcanic soils giving it a unique character

🌋 Taurasi DOCG (Campania) — Full-bodied Power

Location: province of Avellino, 400-700 m, volcanic tuff + clay

Ripening: very late (late October to early November)

Ageing: 3 years (1 in oak); Riserva 4 years

Style: powerful and full, rich in black fruit, with massive tannins, needing 10-25 years

Flavours: black plum, leather, tobacco, volcanic minerality

Producers: Mastroberardino / Antonio Caggiano

🌋 Aglianico del Vulture Superiore DOCG (Basilicata) — Elegant Minerality

Location: the slopes of the extinct Monte Vulture volcano, on volcanic tuff and ash

Ripening: early November, with elevation lengthening the season

Ageing: 3 years (1 in oak); Riserva 5 years (2 in oak)

Style: elegant and refined, distinctly mineral, tight and age-worthy

Flavours: black cherry, violet, volcanic minerality

Producers: Elena Fucci / Paternoster

slides.11.title: 📊 Six Grapes Compared
slides.11.content:
🔍 From the King of the Fog to the Volcanic Treasures of the South

Each of the six grapes has its own terroir DNA. Keys to choosing: tannin + acid structure sets ageing potential; geography and terroir set the flavour character; winemaking sets the style.

🏔️ Piemonte's Big Three (Nebbiolo / Barbera / Dolcetto)

Nebbiolo (very high tannin + acid, pale colour, needs long ageing) ✦ Barbera (high acid + low tannin, versatile everyday wine) ✦ Dolcetto (low acid + medium-high tannin, light and early-drinking). Three complementary personalities from one region, something for every occasion.

🍇 Veneto's Corvina Ladder

Appassimento creates Italy's most distinctive use of one grape: the same variety → fresh Valpolicella / Ripasso re-passed over pomace / dry Amarone (minimum 14%, long-lived) / sweet Recioto. One grape from everyday wine to legend.

🌋 Central and Southern Stars (Sangiovese + Aglianico)

Sangiovese (Italy's most planted, Brunello as the long-ageing peak, many clones) ✦ Aglianico (the Nebbiolo of the South, volcanic minerality, very late-ripening, full Taurasi vs elegant Vulture). Highly structured grapes that both reward patience.

slides.12.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.12.points.0: ✓ Nebbiolo is Italy's noblest grape, concentrated mainly in Piemonte; a paradox of very high tannin + acid in a pale garnet wine that needs 5-30 years of ageing
slides.12.points.1: ✓ Barolo (both Tortonian and Serravallian soils, powerful, 38 months) vs Barbaresco (mainly Tortonian marl, elegant, 26 months): one grape, two souls, with traditionalist vs modernist winemaking
slides.12.points.2: ✓ Barbera has high acidity and low tannin and pairs with almost anything; in 1982 Giacomo Bologna's "Bricco dell'Uccellone" launched the modern quality Barbera revolution
slides.12.points.3: ✓ Barbera's top pyramid: Nizza DOCG (independent since 2014, the peak) → Asti Superiore DOCG → d'Alba DOC → Monferrato DOC (everyday)
slides.12.points.4: ✓ Dolcetto's name means "sweet" but the wine is dry: an early-ripening everyday Piemonte wine with a signature bitter-almond finish and great value
slides.12.points.5: ✓ Corvina's appassimento ladder: Valpolicella (light) → Ripasso (re-passed over pomace) → Amarone (dry, from dried grapes, minimum 14%) → Recioto (sweet, from dried grapes)
slides.12.points.6: ✓ Sangiovese is Italy's most planted grape (71,000 ha), with many clones and local names: Brunello (Montalcino), Prugnolo Gentile (Montepulciano)
slides.12.points.7: ✓ Brunello di Montalcino DOCG (the peak of Sangiovese): 100% Sangiovese, aged 5 years (Riserva 6), with long ageing potential
slides.12.points.8: ✓ Aglianico is the "Nebbiolo of the South": very late-ripening, highly structured, volcanic minerality — Taurasi DOCG (full-bodied Campania) vs Aglianico del Vulture Superiore DOCG (elegant Basilicata)

slides.13.questions.4.question: What is the main winemaking difference between Barolo's "traditionalists" and "modernists"?
slides.13.questions.4.options.1: B. Type of oak and length of maceration
slides.13.questions.4.explanation: Traditionalists age the wine for a long time in large old Slavonian oak casks; modernists shorten the maceration and use small French oak barrels (barriques).
